principles.text: Avoid shorting a stock or sector into a strong, reclaiming weekly candle after a big rally off the lows — wait for it to reclaim (and then lose) the declining 50 EMA and form a tighter, failed-breakout setup before initiating a short.

The best way to answer your own trading questions is to study the charts yourself — working through your own analysis teaches more (new observations, deeper learning) than simply being handed the answer.
Don't change your process for earnings season — manage entries and active positions the same way regardless of whether a name is reporting earnings.

A structural stop placed just below a rising 9/21 EMA support zone gives a clearly defined, low-cost risk, so a pullback-to-support entry offers favorable risk/reward: small defined loss if wrong, large move if the level holds and price turns back up.

Define risk by stop distance and a fixed risk-per-trade, not by a stock's ADR or beta — position size is derived from the stop distance, so two stocks with very different volatility (e.g. 20% ADR vs 5% ADR) can still carry the same dollar risk.

Prefer spreading size across several smaller positions within the same theme/sector (buying a few small bags of chips instead of one family-size bag) rather than concentrating into a single full-size position, because you don't know in advance which name in the group will actually become the leader — or which one hits its stop.

After a huge, extended uptrend, it's unlikely a stock or sector reverses in a straight line down — even names headed for a real downtrend usually go sideways/base near the highs first, producing failed breakouts or breakdowns to short, rather than falling straight down after a huge move.

In a persistently strong market regime, buying pullbacks into support (9/21 EMA) can be more reliable than waiting for classic tight-range contraction, because strong stocks don't waste time chopping near the lows before resuming higher — adapt entry style to what the current market is actually doing.

To judge whether a sector is gaining strength, scan the whole watchlist/screeners daily and look for several (four-plus) stocks in the same sector or industry acting well together, alongside the sector ETF holding/clustering above its EMAs — breadth across names is more reliable evidence than any single stock's action.

Deeply beaten-down assets that finally find a bottom at a key structural level (e.g. a shakeout back to a prior swing low) can rally very fast off the lows in a 'lockout rally' — watch for confirmation at those key levels rather than assuming continued downside just because a name looks beaten down.
